title: The Probability Lab: Dice Game Designers
subtitle: The Laws of Probability — live with your Enrichment group

learningFocus.summary: Students practise the language and logic of probability — describing outcomes as impossible, unlikely, an even chance, likely or certain — by rolling a real 3D die and testing their ideas against what actually happens. Working live alongside their Enrichment group, they connect the maths to designing a fair dice game, a concrete real-life use of probability that carries straight into today's Micro-Project.

orient.objective: Today you will learn to describe how likely something is to happen — from impossible to certain — using a die.
orient.realLife: You use probability every day without noticing — guessing if it will rain, if your team will win, or how risky a decision feels. Game designers use exactly the same idea to decide how fair or how surprising their game should be.
orient.courseLink: This is today's Primary Enrichment Maths session — Session 55's Laws of Probability — before you design your own dice game.
successCriteria: I can use the words impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain to describe an outcome.
I can test a probability idea by rolling a die and checking what actually happens.
I can use probability to help design a fair dice game.

predict.prompt: Before we roll anything — on one normal six-sided die, which is more likely?

rounds.insight: A die only has faces 1 to 6 — a number bigger than 6 can never appear, no matter how many times you roll.
Every face on the die — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 — is less than 7, so this happens every single roll.
Three faces are even (2, 4, 6) and three are odd (1, 3, 5) — exactly half and half.
Only one face out of six shows a 1 — it can happen, but most rolls won't be a 1.

rounds.event: Rolling a number of 3 or more
rounds.insight: Four faces out of six (3, 4, 5, 6) are 3 or more — more often than not, that's what you'll roll.

explain.prompt: Why is it useful to call something 'unlikely' instead of just saying it 'won't happen'?

options.label: Because unlikely things can still happen, so you shouldn't rule them out completely.
Because 'unlikely' and 'impossible' mean exactly the same thing.
Because probability words don't actually matter in real games.

apply.prompt: You're designing a dice game. Landing on 'Lose a turn' happens only when a player rolls a 1. Out of the 6 numbers on the die, how many trigger it — and how likely is that?
